title: Measuring the Marginal Detection Benefit of Sandboxed Emulation for LLM‑Generated NetOps Artifacts: A Preregistered Paired Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory experiment (study_id f2c3d8b1-7a6e-4a9a-b2c3-5f8e1d2b6c7e) that measured the marginal detection benefit of adding an automated sandboxed-emulation stage to a deterministic validator on LLM-generated intent→configuration artifacts. Under shared_initial_candidate semantics with the declared/requested model "gpt-5-mini" we evaluated Npairs = 720 confirmatory tasks drawn from a deterministic task family covering three abstracted vendor‑CLI families and three topology templates. The deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) detected 719/720 = 0.9986111111111111; the guarded pipeline (validator + sandboxed emulation, with at most one repair invocation per task) detected 720/720 = 1.0. Paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.001388888888888884; exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap percentile CI (10000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.0, 0.004166666666666667]. Model-call accounting shows 721 hosted model calls (720 shared initial + 1 repair). These artifact-grounded results fall far below our preregistered minimum effect-of-interest (0.20). We report the preregistered design, exact quantitative outcomes, a methods clarification that reconciles provider-call audit fields, an artifact-grounded interpretation for the negligible guarded benefit in this regime, and reproducibility guidance pointing auditors to the canonical archived execution manifest and associated artifact bundle.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) are being proposed to translate operator intent into device configurations and multi-step NetOps workflows. Production use requires high assurance that generated artifacts satisfy syntactic correctness, ordering/workflow constraints, and higher‑order safety invariants (e.g., keep‑one‑uplink‑up). A common mitigation architecture layers deterministic validation and, where warranted, sandboxed emulation and repair: generate → validate → (repair) → execute. Prior surveys and prototype reports advocate such workflow‑centred mitigations but provide limited large‑scale paired measures of the marginal value added specifically by a sandboxed emulation stage when the same initial generated candidate is presented to both conditions [1]–[3].

We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory experiment to answer the narrowly scoped question: under shared_initial_candidate semantics, what is the paired detection‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) between (A) a deterministic validator‑only pipeline and (B) the same deterministic validator followed by automated sandboxed emulation? Our contributions are: (1) a machine‑readable preregistered design and faithful autonomous execution; (2) an artifact‑grounded paired analysis on Npairs = 720; (3) a methods clarification reconciling provider‑call audit fields under the shared_initial_candidate protocol; and (4) an evidence‑based interpretation and operational guidance characterising the boundary conditions where guarded emulation provides substantive incremental coverage.
sections.related_work:
Workflow‑centred mitigation patterns and verification tools have been emphasized in recent NetOps/Agentic AIOps surveys and system reports, which document the practical trend of pairing generation with deterministic validators, emulators, and repair loops to raise operational assurance [1], [2]. Tool papers in adjacent program‑verification and configuration analysis domains show that verifier‑guided loops often improve correctness but that gaps remain for runtime‑dependent behaviors and stateful sequences [2], [3].

Empirical prototype studies report heterogeneous gains from emulation: when validator coverage aligns with the task distribution, emulation adds little; when tasks expose runtime semantics or environment‑specific side effects, emulation can uncover failures outside static rule sets. These prior observations motivated our preregistered paired design and the choice to enforce shared_initial_candidate semantics so that any between‑condition discordance can only arise from downstream guarded‑stage observations or permitted repair activity.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and design. We preregistered a paired binary confirmatory design (study_id f2c3d8b1‑...) with primary estimand paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. The preregistration fixed Npairs = 720 confirmatory samples (planned episodes = 1440), inclusion/exclusion rules, missingness handling (deterministic reseed up to two times for parser failures), a multiplicity plan for exploratory secondary analyses, and a minimum effect-of-interest = 0.20 used for power planning.

Task bank, vendors, and topology templates. Confirmatory items were deterministically generated from an intent_configuration_repair_v1 task family. The bank spans three abstracted vendor‑CLI families and three topology templates (leaf–spine, 3‑node service chain, triangle). Each task manifest encodes initial_state, expected_final_state, an explicit intent, required_command_sequence, allowed_touched_fields, and workflow policies (e.g., make‑before‑break). Inclusion required vendor‑parser acceptance after up to two deterministic reseeds; in the confirmatory execution there were zero irrecoverable parser exclusions and complete_pair_count = 720.

Model, sampling semantics, and shared_initial_candidate enforcement. The declared/requested model was recorded as "gpt-5-mini" (provider recorded as openai_responses). The preregistered shared_initial_candidate contract produced exactly one sampled initial candidate per task; that identical candidate was presented to both downstream conditions (baseline and guarded). This isolates downstream guarded‑stage effects (emulation observations or permitted repair) as the sole source of between‑condition discordance.

Baseline validator and guarded pipeline. The baseline validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) is a deterministic rule‑based checker that performs vendor‑CLI parsing, canonicalization, sequence‑order checks against required_command_sequence, atomicity/workflow constraints, protected‑interface invariants, group activity constraints, and final‑state conformance tests. It returns a binary detection flag under the scoring rule full_intent_constraint_validation and emits a validator_trace object (validation_before/after, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, violation_codes).

The guarded pipeline runs the baseline validator and then executes the same candidate in an automated sandboxed emulator that instantiates the declared topology and executes normalized CLI commands against vendor‑abstracted virtual devices. The emulator records runtime observations (interface transitions, transient concurrent states, MTU/VLAN application effects, and topology‑level reachability) and maps those observations to runtime‑observation rules that can trigger additional guarded detections. The emulation mapping is intentionally conservative: it flags only runtime effects that indicate policy or safety violations not codified in the static validator.

Repair policy and run accounting. The preregistered repair policy permitted at most one repair‑stage model invocation per task and allowed repairs only after the shared initial candidate was generated and, in the guarded condition, after emulator observations were available. Provider‑call accounting in the execution manifest reports model_calls_used = 721 with stage_counts showing shared_initial_generation = 720 and repair = 1.

Provider‑call audit fields and asymmetry clarification (required revision). To avoid ambiguity we explicitly define the audited fields and reconcile apparent asymmetries under shared_initial_candidate semantics. The provider_call_audit summary reports: (a) hosted_model_call_event_count — total hosted model calls observed during the run (here 721); (b) stage_counts — counts of model calls per pipeline stage (shared_initial_generation = 720, repair = 1 in our run); and (c) condition_counts — model calls attributed to downstream conditions. Under the shared_initial_candidate protocol the single shared initial generation call per pair is executed once and is logically shared by both conditions; auditing therefore records that call in the stage_counts (shared_initial_generation = 720) and also attributes it to the logical "shared" category in condition_counts. Additional calls that run only for the guarded pipeline (repair invocations) appear in stage_counts under "repair" and in condition_counts under "guarded." Thus an apparent asymmetry (condition_counts showing non‑equal numbers) is expected: the shared initial call is counted once in hosted_model_call_event_count but conceptually supplies both baseline and guarded conditions; extra guarded repair calls increase hosted_model_call_event_count above the per‑pair count. Deterministic reconciliations in the archived manifest confirm complete_pair_count = 720, hosted_model_call_event_count = 721 (720 shared + 1 repair), and zero failed model calls. This explanation uses the archived provider_call_audit summary as authoritative and avoids per‑episode log excerpts in the manuscript body.

Analysis procedures. The pre-registered primary analysis uses a paired‑binary executor aligned with McNemar‑style inference. We computed the paired detection‑rate difference (guarded − baseline), performed an exact two‑sided McNemar test, and derived a 95% paired‑bootstrap percentile CI (10000 resamples, seed = 1729) per the preregistered plan. Secondary exploratory per‑class/vendor paired analyses were prespecified but are reported as exploratory with multiplicity corrections.
sections.results:
Primary confirmatory counts and inferential outputs (artifact‑grounded). The analysis contingency counts are: n11 = 719 (detected by both), n10 = 1 (guarded‑only), n01 = 0 (baseline‑only), n00 = 0 (detected by neither). Marginal detection rates: baseline = 719/720 = 0.9986111111111111; guarded = 720/720 = 1.0. Paired estimate (guarded − baseline) = 0.001388888888888884. Exact McNemar two‑sided test p = 1.0. Paired‑bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.0, 0.004166666666666667]. Complete_pair_count = 720; hosted model calls observed = 721 (720 shared_initial_generation + 1 repair), consistent with the preregistered repair policy.

Discordant‑pair attribution. Under shared_initial_candidate semantics and the recorded stage_counts (shared_initial_generation = 720, repair = 1), the single n10 discordant pair must be attributable to either an emulation observation that the static validator did not encode or to the single recorded repair invocation. The archived per‑episode artifacts in the canonical execution manifest allow an auditor to locate that unique pair_id and inspect its validator_trace and any repair transcript; we do not reproduce per‑file logs or hashes in the manuscript body but direct readers to the canonical archived execution manifest and associated artifact bundle for full per‑episode traces.

Representative diagnostics. Representative per‑episode validator_trace outputs from multiple task examples show parsed_command_count, required_command_count, and violation_count = 0 for the vast majority of shared_initial candidates; these representative traces illustrate that the large baseline success rate arises from close alignment between the curated task patterns and the validator rule set.
sections.discussion:
Why the guarded marginal benefit was negligible. Three artifact‑grounded factors explain the near‑zero aggregate effect:

1) Validator ceiling effect and task‑rule alignment. The deterministic validator encoded the key syntactic and workflow checks exercised by the curated tasks (e.g., shutdown_configure_restore, make_before_break_uplink_switchover, paired_link_atomic_mtu_change). The baseline success rate (719/720 ≈ 0.9986) leaves virtually no headroom for the guarded emulator to add detections in this constrained regime.

2) Curated, parser‑validated sample bank. Inclusion required vendor‑parser acceptance and deterministic generation, producing a low‑noise sample set in which many runtime‑only faults that emulation would detect in adversarial or uncurated distributions are underrepresented.

3) Shared_initial_candidate semantics and limited repair activity. Because the identical sampled candidate was used by both conditions, any discordance must originate downstream (emulation or repair). The execution manifest records only a single repair call across all pairs, matching the single observed n10 discordant case.

Operational implications. For operator environments that maintain high‑coverage static validators tailored to expected intent patterns and that enforce parser validation at ingress, adding an automated sandboxed emulator may yield negligible incremental detection coverage at scale. Conversely, guarded emulation remains valuable in regimes with noisy natural‑language intents, adversarial inputs, broader vendor/CLI diversity, or long‑lived stateful interactions. Practical deployment should therefore be guided by the operator’s task distribution and risk posture: (a) invest in richer static validators for high‑throughput, low‑latency scenarios; (b) apply guarded sandboxing selectively for high‑risk changes; (c) use adversarial testbanks to identify validator gaps. The archived run artifacts provide concrete seed cases for such adversarial extensions.

Limitations and scope of inference. This result is narrowly scoped to the preregistered task bank, the single validator implementation, the declared/requested model family, and shared_initial_candidate semantics. The study was powered to detect a minimum paired difference of 0.20; the observed difference (~0.0014) lies far below that sensitivity and therefore should be interpreted as a near‑zero finding specific to this experimental regime rather than a general negative claim about guarded pipelines.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory experiment comparing a deterministic validator with the same validator augmented by sandboxed emulation on a curated synthetic intent→configuration task bank. Over 720 paired tasks the guarded pipeline produced a negligible aggregate detection gain (0.001388888888888884) with exact McNemar p = 1.0 and 95% bootstrap CI [0.0, 0.004166666666666667]. Provider‑call accounting shows 721 hosted model calls (720 shared initial + 1 repair) and reconciles the unique guarded‑only detection to a single downstream event. The most parsimonious, artifact‑grounded interpretation is that a validator closely aligned to the curated task patterns absorbs almost all detectable faults; guarded emulation yields little marginal benefit in this constrained regime. Future work should target adversarial and production‑like task banks, multi‑validator ensembles, and higher‑fidelity emulation to identify regimes where guarded stages add substantive operational value.

disclosure_statement: Disclosure: This study was executed autonomously after an autonomy lock under the supplied master prompt. Declared/requested model: "gpt-5-mini" (provider recorded as openai_responses). Deterministic validator used: deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Orchestration adapter family: hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Preregistration id: f2c3d8b1-7a6e-4a9a-b2c3-5f8e1d2b6c7e (preregistration recorded prior to execution). Human role and autonomy boundary: a human Research Director selected the broad NetOps topic family and constrained the pre‑lock master prompt; after the autonomy lock the agentic pipeline autonomously performed literature review, preregistration, code and prompt generation, experiment execution, analysis, peer review, and manuscript drafting with no manual human editing of technical content after the lock. Immutable initial master‑prompt reference archived in the execution bundle: provenance/master_prompt.txt, SHA‑256 = 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba. The canonical execution manifest and the full archived artifact bundle contain per‑episode traces, provider‑call audit summaries, and binary/configuration version records needed for full reproducibility; readers and auditors should consult that single archived execution manifest in the submission materials for detailed per‑file provenance rather than file excerpts in the paper body.
limitations: Synthetic, deterministic task bank and parser‑validated inclusion produced limited ecological diversity and induced a validator‑ceiling effect; results may not generalize to noisier, adversarial, or production distributions.
Single declared/requested model family (gpt‑5‑mini as recorded) and a single validator implementation (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) limit generalizability across models and validator families.

Preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics (one initial generation per pair reused across conditions) isolate guarded‑stage contributions but remove any generation variability benefit that independent guarded re‑generation could provide.
Sandboxed emulation fidelity is limited by the emulator used; higher‑fidelity emulators modelling vendor control‑plane subtleties or long‑lived state transitions could produce different outcomes.

The study's power planning targeted a minimum detectable paired difference of 0.20; the observed aggregate effect (~0.0014) lies far below that threshold and should be interpreted as a narrowly scoped near‑zero finding for this experimental regime.

Residual provider‑side nondeterminism and hidden caching are practical uncertainties despite deterministic reconciliation and provider‑call auditing; those residual uncertainties and their summaries are archived in the canonical execution manifest for auditors.
